vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
vocab.hint: Tap a word, then tap its meaning

h

paras: 4.1 Data transfer. Invoice data is sent to the ERP once every twenty-four hours, in a single overnight window. Files are validated on arrival and rejected if a mandatory field is missing. Rejected files are held for seven days and are not processed again automatically.

4.2 Access and approval. Access to the production environment is granted only after the security review is complete and the security team has signed off. All configuration changes are approved by the finance team before they are released, and nothing is deleted without a written request. Logs are kept for twelve months and are made available to the auditor on request.

4.3 Availability and maintenance. The platform is expected to comply with the availability standard set out in Annex B. Maintenance is carried out inside a two-hour window, once a month, on a Sunday. This window is fixed and is not negotiated for individual suppliers, and no exceptions have been granted in the last three years.

4.4 Scope, milestones and dependencies. Historic data migration is excluded from this section and is dealt with separately. Three milestones are defined: connection established, one full month validated, and go-live. Each milestone is signed off in writing. The supplier is reminded that a firewall rule change is required on the customer side before the connection can be tested, and that the estimate in Annex C is based on the assumption that supplier files arrive in a single format.

items: The document says who sends the invoice data.
The text says 'Invoice data is sent to the ERP once every twenty-four hours'. It never names who sends it, which is exactly the question to ask.
A rejected file is processed again by the system without anybody doing anything.
The text says rejected files 'are held for seven days and are not processed again automatically'.
Two separate approvals are described in section 4.2.
The text says access is granted after the security team 'has signed off', and that configuration changes 'are approved by the finance team'.
The maintenance window can be moved for an important supplier.
The text says the window 'is fixed and is not negotiated for individual suppliers, and no exceptions have been granted in the last three years'.
Something on the customer side has to happen before the connection can be tested.
The text says 'a firewall rule change is required on the customer side before the connection can be tested'.

items.situation: The document says the data is sent every night. What do you ask?
tips: Can I just check who sends the file?
The sentence has no person in it, and at signature it will find one.

items.situation: Say that the nightly transfer needs no extra work, in the passive.
tips: The nightly transfer is supported as standard.
Is plus the participle, and no by, because who supports it is obvious.

items.situation: Historic migration is real work you have not priced. Say it without saying no.
tips: Historic data migration is not included in the scope and is priced separately.
The negative of the passive: is not plus the participle.

items.situation: Turn this into the passive: they keep the logs for twelve months.
tips: The logs are kept for twelve months.
Keep is irregular: kept, not keeped.

items.situation: You need to know whether the data is protected while it is stored. Ask it.
tips: Is the data encrypted at rest?
A passive question: is plus subject plus participle.

items.situation: Name the line that belongs to the customer, and say why it matters.
tips: The firewall rule change is a dependency on their team.
Twenty minutes of work and six weeks of waiting, because it is on nobody's list.

listenings.text: Eleven pages, one hour, and I read it three times. The first pass is for what is excluded, because that is where the money is, and it is usually one line in the middle of a paragraph. The second pass is the one nobody does. I mark every sentence that does not say who does the thing. The data is sent, access is granted, the file is validated. Every one of those will be assigned to somebody at signature, and if you did not ask, the somebody is you. The third pass is dates and dependencies, and I read those with a pen, because a date with nobody attached to it is not a date. One more thing, and I have made this mistake myself. Watch the word standard. Standard means standard for them, not standard for you, and it is the word I ask about more than any other.

Projects are almost never late because of the work. The work is usually estimated correctly, by people who have done it many times before. They are late because of something nobody wrote down. My favourite example, and I have seen it four times, is a firewall rule change on the customer side. It is twenty minutes of work and six weeks of waiting, because it sits between two teams and it is on nobody's list. That is a dependency, and if it is not in the document it does not exist. And then there is the sentence I hear at every unhappy meeting: the estimate was wrong. The estimate was not wrong. The assumption was. And the difference matters, because a wrong estimate is a mistake somebody has to apologise for, and a wrong assumption is a conversation both sides can have, as long as somebody had the courage to write it down at the beginning.
